title: George Boole and the Algebra of Logic (1854)
explainer: In 1854 the self-taught English mathematician George Boole published An Investigation of the Laws of Thought, showing that logical statements — AND, OR, NOT — could be manipulated with algebraic symbols much like ordinary arithmetic. For decades his system was treated as a curiosity in pure logic with no practical use. It only became the foundation of digital electronics in the 1930s–40s, when engineers realized switching circuits obey the exact same rules — which is why every AND/OR/NOT gate in a computer today is called 'Boolean logic.'

title: Georg Cantor and the Birth of Set Theory (1870s)
explainer: Treating collections as mathematical objects you can compare, one to another, wasn't always obvious or accepted. In the 1870s the German mathematician Georg Cantor founded what became modern set theory, controversially proving that some infinite sets are literally larger than others and introducing the one-to-one correspondence idea this lesson's set operations rest on. His ideas were fiercely resisted by contemporaries, including his own former teacher, but by the 20th century they had become bedrock that most of modern mathematics is built on.
